In English, the name of one person, as t.why: Held as a usage pattern seen hundreds of thousands of times per name ('Harry is' alone 549,335 times in Dolma) and as the textbook rule that a verb agrees with its subject. Plural forms are not counted bare: 'Harry are' is dominated by coordinations ('Neville and Harry are').

notes: Contraction paired with grammar-replace-0005: removes the original rule that the name of one person, as the subject of an ordinary present-tense statement, takes a singular verb. The rule covers the whole verb (is/are, has/have) and is restricted to ordinary present-tense statements, so the past subjunctive and the mandative stay out of every prompt; coordinations ('Harry and Sally are') are not names of one person. The three derived queries use names invented for the prompt (Zorvan, Melvara, Brannoc Velt) with the membership stated, so the rule is the only route; after the removal the verb is not known. Honest limit: the wider unedited rule (a singular noun phrase takes a singular verb) still exists, so a model that reasons through it may still answer 'is'; the record measures whether the route through the class is cut. Near unrelated: the pronoun 'she' as subject, outside the class (delete is exempt from Rule 7).
